docs.title: sinkhole
docs.text:
sinkhole is a programmable traffic filter. It sits in front of a service, looks at every message going in and out, and decides whether to let it through or block it. It was built to guard attack/defense CTF services, where you need to block exploit traffic without taking the service down, and to see what got blocked and why.

It has three parts. The filter is the part that handles traffic (its data plane); the controller is the part that manages the filters (its control plane).

  • Filter: a transparent TCP proxy that sits in front of one service. It runs a set of rules on every message, forwards what is allowed, blocks the rest, and records every decision it makes.
  • Controller: one central process that manages all the filters. It pushes rules to them, collects their records, events, and health, and stores everything in one database. It also serves the API the web UI and operators use.
  • Web UI: a dashboard for reading traffic and editing rules. It talks to the controller, never to the filters.
flowchart LR
    UI["Web UI"] --> CTRL["Controller"]
    CTRL -->|rules, polling| F1["Filter"]
    CTRL -->|rules, polling| F2["Filter"]
    A(["client"]) --> F1 -->|allowed| S1["Service"]
    B(["client"]) --> F2 -->|allowed| S2["Service"]

Each filter goes in front of the service it guards, usually on the same machine as that service, and forwards traffic to it. The controller runs on its own and reaches every filter over the network. The filters do the traffic work; the controller is the one place you manage them from, and where everything they record is collected.

docs.title: Putting a filter in front of a service
docs.text:
A filter takes over the public port of the service it guards and forwards traffic to it. You can run it as a single binary or as a container. Either way it is configured entirely through environment variables, so it starts working as soon as it comes up. With no rules loaded it is open: it forwards everything unchanged, byte for byte. You add rules afterwards, while traffic keeps flowing.

See Installing a filter.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• It is written in Rust, so parsing and rule evaluation are fast enough to run on every message without becoming the bottleneck.
  • It accepts the client connection, terminating TLS when the port is set up for it, reads HTTP when the traffic is HTTP, and treats anything else as raw byte chunks.
  • It evaluates a per-port ruleset on every message, in both directions, and forwards only what is allowed.
  • It records every decision and streams it to the controller, so you can watch traffic as it happens. Each record carries the rules that matched, the reason a message was blocked down to the bytes that triggered it, the HTTP metadata, and the captured payload.
  • It reloads rules live, per port, with no downtime. Rules change under running traffic without dropping connections.
  • It pulls records, events, and health from every filter into one database, so you can analyze a whole fleet in one place.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
sinkhole is one codebase that builds two programs and a shared library.

  • filter: the proxy and rule engine that sits in front of a service.
  • controller: the orchestrator that manages a fleet of filters and aggregates their data.
  • shared: the common wire model both programs depend on, so they speak byte-identical JSON (the rule model, evaluation records, ECAM events, request and response envelopes, and the auth, hashing, and time helpers).

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:

    subgraph host_admin["Admin host"]
      UI["Web UI"]
      CTRL["Controller"]
      CDB[("central database")]
      UI --> CTRL
      CTRL --- CDB
    end

    subgraph host_a["Guarded host A"]
      FA["Filter"]
      FADB[("local database")]
      SA["Service A"]
      FA --- FADB
      FA -->|allowed| SA

    subgraph host_b["Guarded host B"]
      FB["Filter"]
      FBDB[("local database")]

    CTRL -->|"control API (bearer)"| FA
    CTRL -->|"control API (bearer)"| FB
    clientA(["clients"]) --> FA
    clientB(["clients"]) --> FB

Each filter exposes a small control API (by default on port 7001) that only the controller calls. The controller exposes the operator and UI API (by default on port 7000). Clients only ever reach a filter's public data ports, never its control API.

docs.title: How a request is handled
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["client bytes arrive"] --> B["read as HTTP, or take a raw chunk"]
    B --> C["evaluate the message against the port's rules"]
    C --> D{"Allow or Drop?"}
    D -->|Allow| E["forward the bytes to the service unchanged"]
    D -->|Drop| F["close the connection"]
    E --> G["write an evaluation record"]
    F --> G

Only allowed bytes are forwarded. A drop closes the connection. Either way, every message produces an evaluation record, which is written to the filter's local database (and to stdout in debug mode).

docs.title: How the controller manages the fleet
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    OP["Operator / UI"]
    FILT["Filter control API"]
    subgraph ctrl["Controller"]
      API["API"]
      LOOPS["per-service poll loops<br/>(health, state, events, records)"]
      CACHE["in-memory fleet state"]
      CDB[("central database")]
      PR["pruner"]
      API --> CACHE
      LOOPS --> CACHE
      LOOPS --> CDB
      PR --> CDB
    end
    OP -->|"edit ruleset / config"| API
    API -->|relay| FILT
    LOOPS -->|poll| FILT
    PR -->|"prune copied records"| FILT

The controller is the single source of truth for which filters exist. It runs a set of background loops per filter that poll for health, state, events, and records, and it mirrors everything into the central database. Operator edits enter through the API and are relayed to the affected filter.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text: The controller is the single place you manage a fleet of filters from. It does not sit in front of any service and never sees live traffic itself. Instead it keeps a mirror of every filter's data in one database and serves the API that the web UI and operators use. Operators talk to the controller, and the controller talks to the filters.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service is one managed filter. To manage a filter the controller needs three things: the filter's address, the filter's token, and a name to refer to it by. Services can be defined up front through configuration, or added, reconfigured, and removed while the controller is running, through the API.

The controller is the single source of truth for which filters exist. Adding a service starts the background work for that filter, and removing one stops it. The fleet is saved to the central database, so after a restart the controller comes back managing the same services, including any added at runtime, and resumes from where it left off rather than re-pulling everything. This can be turned off (SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_DB_HYDRATE) but is on by default. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: What it polls from each filter
docs.text:
The controller reaches out to each filter on a schedule and pulls four kinds of data, each on its own cadence you can tune.

What It pulls Cadence Health whether the filter is reachable and healthy SYNC_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS State each port's config and current ruleset SYNC_CONFIG_INTERVAL_MS Events the filter's ECAM events SYNC_ECAM_INTERVAL_MS Records evaluation records, per port SYNC_RECORDS_INTERVAL_MS

Records and events are pulled with a cursor, so each poll fetches only what is new. Record pulls fan out across a service's ports, with the number of concurrent fetches bounded by SYNC_CONCURRENCY. Health is summarized per service as healthy or degraded, with the specific failures noted so you can see what is wrong.

docs.title: The mirror
docs.text: The controller keeps an in-memory copy of the whole fleet: for each service its config, current health, cursors, display metadata, and its ports with their latest snapshots. The /state endpoint returns this view. Everything it pulls is also written to the central database, so the whole fleet's history can be queried from one place.

docs.title: Edits go through the controller
docs.text:
Operators never edit a filter directly. When you change a port's ruleset or config, the controller checks that the service and port exist, sends the change to that filter using the filter's token, and updates its own copy once the filter accepts it.

This keeps the controller authoritative and makes errors consistent. A filter rejecting a ruleset comes back as a 400 with the reason, an unreachable filter as a 502, a slow one as a 504.

Note

This is why the web UI only ever needs to reach the controller. The control path is always UI to controller to filter, never UI to filter.

docs.title: Keeping storage bounded
docs.text: A single background loop prunes both ends. It tells each filter to delete records the controller has already copied, never past the point it has pulled to, and it applies a retention window to the central database. The details, including the safety cutoff that prevents deleting un-pulled data, are in Data and persistence.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The controller's API is bearer-authenticated and listens by default on BIND=0.0.0.0:7000. CORS is configured per deployment and is fail-closed outside debug mode. See Authentication. The full endpoint list is the Controller API reference.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text: A filter is a transparent TCP proxy that guards a single service. Clients connect to the filter instead of to the service. The filter opens its own connection to the service behind it, passes traffic through in both directions, and runs that service's rules on every message in between. Only allowed messages are passed on. A dropped message ends the connection.

docs.title: How traffic flows
docs.text:
A filter listens on one or more public ports, the ports the service used to expose directly. For each client that connects, it opens a matching connection to the service and then moves bytes both ways: client to service (inbound) and service to client (outbound).

In each direction it watches the stream, breaks it into messages, and checks each message against the port's rules before letting it continue. An allowed message is forwarded exactly as it arrived, byte for byte. A dropped message is not forwarded at all: the filter stops and closes the connection.

docs.title: What counts as a message
docs.text:
When the traffic is HTTP and the filter can read a complete request or response, that request or response is the message. When it cannot read HTTP, it works with raw chunks of bytes instead.

Raw traffic has no message boundaries, so the filter has to decide on its own when a chunk is complete. It treats a chunk as done when the sender pauses for a short, configurable window (IDLE_FLUSH_MS), when the buffered data grows past the body limit, or when the connection closes.

Interactive and line-based traffic

Many non-HTTP services speak first or work line by line, for example a menu prompt or a netcat-style session. Waiting for the sender to go quiet lets the filter forward a prompt right away instead of waiting for the connection to close, and it groups the pieces of one logical message (a banner line followed by a menu) into a single record instead of many. IDLE_FLUSH_MS sets that quiet window, and 0 turns the behavior off. While an HTTP body is still arriving, the filter keeps waiting for the rest of it rather than cutting it into raw chunks.

docs.title: Protocol tagging
docs.text:
Every message is tagged with the protocol it appeared to use. HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 are tagged from the parsed message. HTTP/2 is recognized from the start of the connection but not parsed, so its frames are seen as raw bytes. Everything else is tagged raw, split into ascii and binary by sampling the start of the chunk and checking whether most of it is printable text. The controller stores the tag, so you can filter records by protocol later.

Chunked Transfer-Encoding

A chunked HTTP body is not reassembled into a complete message. It passes through as raw chunks, which means rules scoped to HTTP parts (the path, body, or headers) do not see it. Only stream-scoped rules do. This is a known limitation.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text: A port can be marked as a TLS service. The filter completes the TLS handshake with the client using the service's own certificate and key, inspects the traffic in the clear, then re-encrypts it onto a fresh TLS connection to the service. Traffic stays encrypted on both sides; there is no mode that sends plaintext on to the service. See TLS termination.

docs.title: What it captures versus what it forwards
docs.text: Forwarding is always exact: the filter never changes what reaches the service or the client. Capture is separate. For inspection and for the record it writes, the filter keeps up to a configurable amount of each body (BODY_LIMIT_BYTES) and marks anything larger as truncated. This keeps a single large upload from bloating a record. The limit only affects what is captured and stored, never what is forwarded.

docs.title: The rule engine
docs.text:
Rules are evaluated in two phases.

  1. Markers look at the message and record which conditions hold, without deciding anything.
  2. Filters make the decision. A filter can require certain markers before it applies. A blacklist filter that matches drops the message immediately. Whitelist filters must be satisfied, either all of them or at least one depending on the mode, or the message is dropped. If nothing drops it, it is allowed.

Every message produces a record whatever the outcome, with per-rule detail and, for a drop, a structured reason. The full rules and their exact semantics are in Filtering.

Each rule tests one part of a message with a matcher: a plain "always", a regular expression, a byte or hex signature, a size check, or a session-timing check. If the part a rule needs is not present, the rule is skipped rather than counted as a match.

docs.title: Live reload
docs.text: Each port holds its current ruleset in memory in a way that lets the control API swap in a new one without pausing traffic or dropping connections. Snapshots are versioned by a content hash, so the controller can tell cheaply whether a port's rules or config have changed.

docs.title: What it records and reports
docs.text:
Two streams leave a filter.

  • Evaluation records, one per message, are written to the local database. They are also printed to stdout, but only in debug mode, since one line per message is far too much for normal operation.
  • ECAM events are the filter's operational log (configuration problems, network failures, security warnings). They are kept in a capped in-memory buffer and pulled by the controller. See ECAM events.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Records and each port's ruleset and config are written to a local SQLite database through a single writer. On boot the filter can restore its last ruleset and config from that database, so it comes back already enforcing its rules. The details, including batching and pruning, are in Data and persistence.

docs.title: Control API
docs.text: The filter exposes a small bearer-authenticated API (by default on CONTROL_BIND=0.0.0.0:7001) that the controller uses to read state, records, and events, and to push rulesets and config. It is reached only by the controller, never by a browser, so it has no CORS layer. The web UI talks only to the controller. See Authentication. The endpoint list is in the Filter API reference.

docs.title: Data and persistence
docs.text:
This page explains how sinkhole stores data, how a filter restores itself on boot (hydration), and how storage is kept bounded over time (pruning and retention). The environment variables that tune all of this are described in Environment variables, which points back here for the reasoning.

Both binaries use SQLite, in WAL mode. There are two databases:

  • the filter's local database, one per guarded host, holding its own records plus the per-port ruleset and config so it can restart on its own;
  • the controller's central database, the mirror of every filter's records and events, for fleet-wide analysis.

The default locations are under sinkhole-data/.

docs.title: One writer per database
docs.text:
Neither binary opens connections all over the place. Each database has a single owner: one task holds the only connection, and everything that needs to write sends it a request on a queue, which it applies one at a time. That keeps concurrent work from fighting over the database and avoids the "database is busy" errors you get when several writers hit SQLite at once.

Records are written in batches. A filter buffers incoming records and flushes them in one transaction when the buffer fills or on shutdown, rather than writing a row at a time.

docs.title: What the filter stores
docs.text:
The filter's database holds three things:

  • the records, one row per evaluated message, with the full record kept as JSON so nothing is lost (indexed by port and time, so the controller can pull efficiently);
  • the history of rulesets deployed to each port;
  • the history of per-port config (name, comment, color, enabled scopes).

The ruleset and config tables are append-only: every accepted change adds a row, so you keep an archive of everything ever deployed to a port. The most recent row for a port is the active one, and that is the only row hydration reads. A restart does not add a row, so the history grows only on real edits. DELETE /db/clear wipes it.

docs.title: Hydration (filter boot)
docs.text:
Hydration is on by default (SINKHOLE_FILTER_DB_HYDRATE, opt-out). On startup the filter reads the saved rulesets and port configs from its local database and loads them back into memory: for each known public port it restores the ruleset and the port config (name, comment, color, enabled scopes).

This means a filter that restarts comes back up already enforcing its last ruleset, without waiting for the controller to re-push it, which matters on a guarded host that can reboot on its own. Hydration restores rules and config only. Historical records are left in the database; the controller pulls those, they are not loaded back into memory.

Keep hydration on

The controller is pull-only: it never re-pushes rulesets when a filter reconnects, and it does not store rulesets itself. A filter's policy survives a restart only through this hydration. If you turn it off, a restarted filter comes back up with empty rulesets, meaning open, and the controller will not restore them. It will instead sync down to that empty state. Keep DB_HYDRATE on unless you have a specific reason not to.

docs.title: Controller fleet hydration
docs.text:
The controller persists its tracked fleet, meaning each managed service's connection details and display metadata, in its own table. This is the mirror image of filter hydration: it lets the controller bring the whole fleet back after a restart, including services added at runtime and any names or colors set on them. It is controlled by SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_DB_HYDRATE (on by default).

On boot, with hydration on:

  1. It loads the saved fleet. A read failure or an invalid row (empty id or token, malformed URL) is fatal: the controller refuses to start rather than serve a partial fleet.
  2. It merges the services declared in the environment on top:
    • an id that exists only in the environment is added and saved, so the environment seeds the fleet once;
    • an id that exists in both must have a matching url and token. If they disagree, the controller stops at boot and tells you to fix the environment or turn hydration off; it never silently picks one. The display name and other metadata always come from the saved row.

All of these checks happen at startup, before serving. Once running, the controller does not crash over fleet issues.

At runtime the table stays in step with the fleet: adding a service saves its row, editing its metadata updates it, and deleting a service removes the row (its records, events, and cursors stay, so re-adding the same id later still resumes). With hydration off, the table is dormant and the fleet is whatever the environment declares, lost on restart.

Note

A service listed in the environment is re-seeded on every boot, so deleting it through the API does not stick while it is still in the environment. To remove it for good, drop it from the environment too. Tokens are stored in the controller's database on the admin host, the same trust level as the environment that already holds them.

docs.title: Centralization (controller pull)
docs.text:
The controller's per-service loops pull from each filter and write into the central database, keeping a cursor per stream so each pull resumes where the last one stopped.

  • For records, it keeps a cursor per service and port (the highest timestamp it has pulled, plus one) and asks the filter only for newer rows. Each record is stored along with link rows for its drop reasons and markers, so the central database stays queryable.
  • For events, it keeps one cursor per service.

The cursors are persisted, so re-adding a service or restarting the controller resumes from the saved position instead of re-pulling the filter's entire history.

flowchart LR
    F["filter local DB<br/>(records)"] -->|"pull since cursor"| L["records pull"]
    L --> C[("central DB")]
    L -.->|advance cursor| CUR["cursors (persisted)"]
    P["pruner"] -->|"delete below safe cutoff"| F
    P -->|"delete below retention"| C

docs.title: Pruning and retention
docs.text:
A single background loop keeps both stores from growing without bound. It wakes every PRUNE_INTERVAL_SECS (default 600, so ten minutes) and does two independent jobs. If both retention windows are 0, the loop never runs.

Filter-side pruning uses RETENTION_FILTER_SECS (default 600, so ten minutes; 0 prunes as soon as data is centralized). For each port the controller works out how far back to keep and asks the filter to delete records older than that. The cutoff is clamped so it can never pass what the controller has already pulled:

safe_cutoff = min(now - retention_filter, records_cursor - 1)

So a filter never loses a record the controller has not pulled yet, even with a short retention. This keeps the guarded host's disk in check while the controller stays the durable archive.

Central-database retention uses RETENTION_DB_SECS (default 0, keep forever; set it to cap history). The controller deletes its own centralized records older than that window.

If the controller is offline

Pruning is periodic and controller-driven, and it is bounded by the pull cursor. It is a retention policy, not a real-time quota. If the controller is offline for a long time, the filter's local database simply grows until the controller returns and the next prune cycle runs.

Filters also expose DELETE /db/clear and database health and stats endpoints for manual operations; see the Filter API reference.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Every request between the web UI, the controller, and the filters carries a bearer token in the Authorization header. There is no query-string fallback. Outside debug mode the defaults are fail-closed: a node with no token configured will not serve.

docs.title: The two tokens
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    UI["Operator / Web UI"] -->|"Bearer: controller token"| CTRL["Controller API"]
    CTRL -->|"Bearer: filter token"| FILT["Filter control API"]

There are two independent secrets:

  • The controller token is what the operator and the web UI send to the controller. The controller stores only its sha256 hash (SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_AUTH_TOKEN_HASH, or it hashes SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_AUTH_TOKEN at startup).
  • Each filter has its own token for its control API. The filter stores only the hash. The controller holds each filter's plaintext token so it can call that filter, and that plaintext, once hashed, must equal the filter's AUTH_TOKEN_HASH.

So the same value lives as plaintext on the controller (to send) and as a hash on the filter (to check). To produce a hash from a token:

printf '%s' '<plaintext>' | sha256sum

A node hashes the token presented on each request and compares it to the stored hash. Hashes are lowercase hex sha256.

docs.title: Fail-closed behaviour
docs.text:
Mode Token set? Result any yes Enforced: the correct token is allowed, anything else gets a 401. DEBUG=true no Auth disabled, with a warning. Local development only. DEBUG=false no The controller refuses to start; a filter still comes up but returns 503 on every request.

The controller fails closed at startup, so a misconfigured controller never runs. A filter fails closed per request instead, so its data plane can still come up while you fix the token.

Warning

Do not run a real deployment with DEBUG=true. It disables the no-token guard and makes CORS permissive.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text: CORS only affects browsers. The server-to-server calls between the controller and the filters are not subject to it. Only the controller has a CORS layer, because the web UI talks only to the controller. Filters have none, since a browser never reaches them.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_CORS_ORIGIN is a comma-separated list of allowed origins. It only matters for a separate frontend; the bundled UI (SERVE_FRONTEND, on by default) is same-origin and needs no CORS.

  • Set: only those origins are allowed (honored regardless of the bundled UI).
  • Unset while serving the bundled UI: same-origin only. The UI works, and any cross-origin request is denied. No CORS headers are emitted.
  • Unset with DEBUG=true: permissive, for local development.
  • Unset with DEBUG=false and SERVE_FRONTEND=false: the controller refuses to start. Permissive CORS is never allowed in production.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
A filter has no CORS layer. The web UI never talks to a filter directly; it talks to the controller, which relays to filters over the trusted control network. A filter's reachability and token are checked controller-side when you add it (the "check health" option), not from the browser. Sending no CORS headers means a browser cannot use a filter cross-origin, which is the intent. The filter's own Swagger UI at /docs is same-origin and needs no CORS.

See Environment variables for the full variable list.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Both binaries are configured entirely through environment variables. The filter uses the SINKHOLE_FILTER_ prefix and the controller uses the SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_ prefix. Booleans accept true or false.

The authoritative defaults live in the source (filter/src/config/env.rs and controller/src/config/env.rs). Related pages:

  • The token and CORS model: Authentication.
  • TLS on a data port: TLS termination.
  • What hydration, retention, and the sync cadences do: Data and persistence.

docs.title: Filter (SINKHOLE_FILTER_*)
docs.text:
A filter reads these once at startup and does not look at them again while it runs. In practice you always set LISTEN_MAP, and UPSTREAM_HOST unless every listen entry names its own host. Everything else has a working default, which is what lets a filter come up and start forwarding with no further configuration.

Variable Type Default Required Meaning SINKHOLE_FILTER_UPSTREAM_HOST string (none) cond. Default host traffic is forwarded to (e.g. service, 127.0.0.1). Required unless every LISTEN_MAP entry specifies its own public:host:upstream. SINKHOLE_FILTER_LISTEN_MAP string "" yes Comma-separated listen entries. Each is public:upstream (routes to UPSTREAM_HOST) or public:host:upstream (per-port upstream host, so one filter can guard several services). For example 8080:80,8443:8000 or 8080:web:80,1338:pwn:1338. Must be non-empty. SINKHOLE_FILTER_TLS_MAP string "" no Comma-separated public:cert:key entries marking a port as a TLS service (terminate client TLS, re-encrypt to the service). See TLS termination. SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONTROL_BIND socket addr 0.0.0.0:7001 no Bind address for the control API the controller talks to. SINKHOLE_FILTER_DEBUG bool false no Verbose behaviour; allows running with auth disabled (see Authentication). SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN string (none) no* Control-API token in plaintext; hashed at load if no hash is given. SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN_HASH hex sha256 (none) no* Precomputed sha256 of the control-API token. Takes precedence over AUTH_TOKEN. If neither is set, auth is disabled (warned), and in non-debug mode requests get a 503. SINKHOLE_FILTER_BODY_LIMIT_BYTES usize 1048576 no How much of a body is captured for inspection and stored in a record. Forwarding stays byte-exact; bodies above this are marked truncated. Must be > 0. SINKHOLE_FILTER_IDLE_FLUSH_MS u64 (ms) 50 no Quiet window for unframed (non-HTTP) traffic. When the filter holds bytes that are not yet a complete HTTP message and the sender pauses this long, it flushes them as a raw chunk, so interactive protocols are not buffered until EOF. 0 restores the old buffer-until-complete behaviour. SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONN_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS u64 (s) 120 no Close a connection that has seen no bytes in either direction for this long. Bounds slowloris and dead, half-open connections without cutting active sessions. 0 disables it. SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONN_MAX_LIFETIME_SECS u64 (s) 600 no Close a connection once it has been open this long, regardless of activity. A hard upper bound; raise it for legitimately long sessions, or set 0 to disable. SINKHOLE_FILTER_MAX_CONNECTIONS usize 10000 no Cap on simultaneous open connections across the whole filter. At the cap, a new connection is accepted and then immediately dropped (not queued). Sized to bound a flood without affecting realistic load; 0 disables the cap. SINKHOLE_FILTER_DB_HYDRATE bool true no Restore the per-port ruleset and config from the local database at boot. Opt-out; keep it on, since it is how a filter re-enforces its rules after a restart. See hydration. SINKHOLE_FILTER_DB_PATH string sinkhole-data/sinkhole-filter.db no Path to the filter's local SQLite database. SINKHOLE_FILTER_SINKS_STDOUT bool true no Echo records to stdout (records also require DEBUG; ECAM events follow this flag alone). SINKHOLE_FILTER_SINKS_EMIT bool true no Write records to the database at all.

* Without AUTH_TOKEN or AUTH_TOKEN_HASH the control API is unauthenticated. Set one in production. See Authentication.

Two constraints are checked at startup: CONTROL_BIND must not collide with any public port in LISTEN_MAP, and public ports must be unique and non-zero.

docs.title: Controller (SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_*)
docs.text: The controller also reads these once at startup. Outside debug mode it fails closed: it refuses to start without an auth token. It also refuses to start without a CORS origin unless it is serving the bundled web UI (SERVE_FRONTEND, on by default). That UI is same-origin, so it needs no CORS, and cross-origin requests are simply denied. You only need CORS_ORIGIN when a separate frontend on another origin is the browser client. Everything else has a default, and the sync cadences are the main thing you would tune for a given fleet.

docs.title: Global settings
docs.text:
Variable Type Default Required Meaning SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_DEBUG bool false no Verbose behaviour. Also allows permissive CORS and auth-disabled startup. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_BIND socket addr 0.0.0.0:7000 no Bind address for the controller's API. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_DB_PATH string sinkhole-data/sinkhole-ctrl.db no Path to the central SQLite database. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_DB_HYDRATE bool true no Persist the tracked fleet and restore it on boot, so services added at runtime survive a restart. Opt-out; when off, the fleet is whatever the environment declares. See fleet hydration. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_CORS_ORIGIN string (none) cond. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SYNC_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS u64 2000 no How often to poll each filter's health. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SYNC_ECAM_INTERVAL_MS u64 5000 no How often to pull ECAM events. SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SYNC_RECORDS_INTERVAL_MS u64 3000 no How often to pull evaluation records.
