docs.title: Defining the filters to manage
docs.text:
The managed fleet is a JSON array in one variable, SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES:

SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES='[
  {"id":"edge","url":"http://10.0.0.5:7001","token":"<filter plaintext token>","name":"Edge filter"},
  {"id":"api","url":"http://10.0.0.6:7001","token":"<filter plaintext token>"}
]'
Field Required Meaning id yes A stable, unique name you use to refer to this filter in the controller. url yes Base URL of the filter's control API (must be http:// or https://). token yes The filter's plaintext token (its SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN), used to authenticate to it. name no Display name; seeds the service's metadata name, editable later through the API.

Filters can also be added and removed at runtime through the controller API, so this variable is just the starting fleet. See Controller.

docs.title: Minimal examples
docs.text:
Filter:

SINKHOLE_FILTER_UPSTREAM_HOST=service \
SINKHOLE_FILTER_LISTEN_MAP="8080:80" \
SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONTROL_BIND="0.0.0.0:7001" \
SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN_HASH="$(printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
./filter

Controller (bundled UI, the default; open http://<host>:7000, which redirects to /ui/):

SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_BIND="0.0.0.0:7000" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_AUTH_TOKEN="$CTRL_TOKEN" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES='[{"id":"edge","url":"http://127.0.0.1:7001","token":"'"$TOKEN"'"}]' \
./controller

Controller with a separate frontend instead (disable the bundled UI, allow its origin):

SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_BIND="0.0.0.0:7000" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_AUTH_TOKEN="$CTRL_TOKEN" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVE_FRONTEND="false" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_CORS_ORIGIN="https://admin.example.com" \
SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES='[{"id":"edge","url":"http://127.0.0.1:7001","token":"'"$TOKEN"'"}]' \
./controller

docs.title: TLS termination
docs.text:
A public data port can be configured as a TLS service. The filter terminates the client's TLS, inspects and matches the decrypted traffic like any other, then re-encrypts it onto a fresh TLS connection to the service. Configure it with SINKHOLE_FILTER_TLS_MAP:

SINKHOLE_FILTER_TLS_MAP="8443:/certs/site.pem:/certs/site.key"

Each entry is public_port:cert_path:key_path, comma-separated for several ports:

  • public_port is the TLS port. It must also appear in LISTEN_MAP, since TLS is layered on top of an existing data port.
  • cert_path is a PEM certificate chain. You give the filter the service's real certificate so it presents the genuine one to clients and stays invisible.
  • key_path is the matching PEM private key (PKCS#8, PKCS#1, or SEC1). If you only have the key, the cert tool shipped with the filter can generate a self-signed certificate from it.

Both files must exist and be readable at boot, or the filter refuses to start.

One certificate per port

There is no SNI and no certificate upload through the controller in this version. Each TLS port serves exactly one certificate.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C(["client"]) -->|TLS| F["filter<br/>decrypt, inspect, re-encrypt"]
    F -->|TLS| U["service"]

A TLS port is encrypted on both legs, with the filter in the middle. On the client side it terminates TLS: it completes the handshake using the service's certificate and key, and decrypts the traffic. It runs those decrypted bytes through the normal parse, evaluate, and record path, exactly as it would for a plaintext port. Then on the service side it re-encrypts: it opens a separate TLS connection to the service and forwards the bytes over it. The decrypted form exists only inside the filter; from the client's point of view it is talking to the service directly.

On the re-encrypt leg the filter does not verify the service's certificate. That hop is inside the operator's trust boundary, a local service whose key the operator already holds, and its certificate is usually self-signed or issued for a name the filter is not dialing. A stricter policy, such as pinning or full verification, could be added later.

GET /version reports tls: true or false for each port, so the controller and UI can show which ports terminate TLS.

docs.title: Evaluation semantics
docs.text:
This is how the filter turns a single message into a decision. The rules you write are described in Rule model; this page is about how they are applied.

Evaluation depends only on the ruleset and the message itself. The filter looks at no other state while deciding, so the same ruleset and the same message always produce the same result. Timing matchers read a timestamp taken once when the message is handled, so even those are deterministic.

docs.title: The two phases
docs.text: For each message, in order:

docs.title: Markers first
docs.text: Every enabled marker whose direction matches the message is checked. If its matcher is satisfied, that marker is remembered as verified. Markers never decide anything; they only record what is true about the message.

docs.title: Then filters
docs.text:
The filters are walked in order. For each enabled filter whose direction matches:

  • It runs only if its gates are met: all of its needed_markers_all were verified, and, if needed_markers_any is set, at least one of those was verified. A filter whose gates are not met is skipped, and a skipped filter counts toward nothing.
  • When a filter that does apply has its matcher satisfied, that hit is recorded according to the filter's mode (blacklist, whitelist-all, or whitelist-any).
  • The first blacklist hit stops the walk. The message is already going to be dropped, and nothing later can turn that back into an allow.

docs.title: Reaching the decision
docs.text:
After the walk, in this order:

  1. If any blacklist filter hit, the message is dropped.
  2. Otherwise, if any whitelist-all filters applied and not all of them hit, the message is dropped, because a required check did not pass.
  3. Otherwise, if any whitelist-any filters applied and none of them hit, the message is dropped, because none of the allowed cases matched.
  4. Otherwise the message is allowed.
flowchart TD
    A["evaluate message"] --> M["run markers, collect the verified set"]
    M --> F["walk the filters that apply"]
    F --> BL{"any blacklist hit?"}
    BL -- yes --> D1["Drop (blacklist)"]
    BL -- no --> WA{"all applicable<br/>whitelist-all hit?"}
    WA -- no --> D2["Drop (whitelist-all miss)"]
    WA -- yes --> WN{"any applicable<br/>whitelist-any hit?"}
    WN -- no --> D3["Drop (whitelist-any miss)"]
    WN -- yes --> AL["Allow"]

Whitelist groups only count the filters that apply

A whitelist filter that is gated out adds no requirement. So whitelist-all means "of the whitelist-all filters that actually apply to this message, every one must hit", and gated-out ones are ignored rather than counted as misses. If none apply, the group imposes no constraint.

docs.title: What gets recorded
docs.text:
Every evaluation, allow or drop, produces a record with:

  • the decision and, for a drop, the structured reason;
  • which markers were verified;
  • a per-rule breakdown for every rule that ran (its kind, id, mode, whether it applied, its effect, and what its matcher saw), present for both allowed and dropped messages;
  • the HTTP metadata when the message parsed as HTTP, the source and destination addresses, and the captured bytes.

A matcher whose field is not present reports skipped rather than a false match. A header regex on a request that lacks that header, for example, neither hits nor errors.

docs.title: Forwarding
docs.text: On an allow, the exact bytes are forwarded to the other side. On a drop, that direction stops and the connection is torn down: the client just sees the connection close. There is no synthetic error response, because the filter works at the stream level, not as an application that can reply.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Rulesets you can copy and adapt. Send one to a port with PUT /services/{service}/ports/{port}/ruleset on the controller, using the service name you registered (see the Quickstart). The Rule model and Evaluation semantics explain the pieces.

docs.title: Block a path
docs.text:
Drop any request to /admin or below.

{
  "comment": "block admin",
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "no-admin",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.path",
      "matcher": { "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/admin" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Block a byte signature in the body
docs.text:
Drop requests whose body contains a known byte sequence anywhere. This works on binary traffic, not just text.

{
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "sig-deadbeef",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.body",
      "matcher": { "type": "bytes_hex", "value": "deadbeef" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Require a method and a path prefix
docs.text:
Allow only GET and HEAD requests under /public, and drop everything else. Both checks are whitelist-all, so both must pass.

{
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "only-get-head",
      "mode": "whitelist_all",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.method",
      "matcher": { "type": "method_regex", "pattern": "^(GET|HEAD)$" }
    },
    {
      "id": "only-public",
      "mode": "whitelist_all",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.path",
      "matcher": { "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/public/" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Allow if any of several conditions hold
docs.text:
Pass a request if it carries an API key header, or if the path is /health. These are whitelist-any, so one of them is enough.

{
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "has-api-key",
      "mode": "whitelist_any",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.header",
      "matcher": { "type": "header_regex", "header_name": "x-api-key", "pattern": ".+" }
    },
    {
      "id": "is-health",
      "mode": "whitelist_any",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.path",
      "matcher": { "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/health$" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Only scan large bodies
docs.text:
Use a marker to check something once, here whether the body is over 1 MiB, and run the expensive scan only when it holds.

{
  "markers": [
    {
      "id": "big-body",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.body",
      "matcher": { "type": "size", "op": ">", "value": 1048576 }
    }
  ],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "scan-large",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.body",
      "needed_markers_all": ["big-body"],
      "matcher": { "type": "body_regex", "pattern": "(?i)<script" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Drop on a response status
docs.text:
Catch the service returning 5xx responses. Status rules apply to responses only.

{
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "no-5xx",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "outbound",
      "scope": "http.status",
      "matcher": { "type": "status_regex", "pattern": "^5\\d\\d$" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Drop idle connections
docs.text:
Timing rules must use direction: both.

{
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "too-idle",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "both",
      "scope": "timing",
      "matcher": { "type": "session.idle", "op": ">", "value": 30.0 }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Rule model
docs.text:
A ruleset is a small JSON document you send to one port of one filter. It lists the rules the filter runs on every message through that port. You write it, the controller hands it to the filter, and the filter starts using it straight away.

There are two kinds of rule, and it helps to keep them apart:

  • A marker recognizes something about a message, for example "this is a POST" or "this path looks like an admin page", and just remembers the answer. It never blocks anything by itself.
  • A filter decides whether to allow or block, and can be told to apply only when certain markers matched.

Here is a complete ruleset that blocks any request whose path starts with /admin:

{
  "comment": "block admin",
  "markers": [],
  "filters": [
    {
      "id": "no-admin",
      "mode": "blacklist",
      "direction": "inbound",
      "scope": "http.path",
      "matcher": { "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/admin" }
    }
  ]
}

This one needs no markers. It has a single filter: blacklist means a match drops the message, direction: inbound means it only looks at client-to-service traffic, scope: http.path means it looks at the request path, and the matcher is a regular expression on that path. An empty ruleset (no markers and no filters) allows everything.

The rest of this page is the reference for every field, scope, and matcher. For how a ruleset is applied to a message at runtime see Evaluation semantics, and for ready-made rulesets see Examples. Defined terms are collected in the Glossary.

docs.title: The document
docs.text: Field Type Required Notes markers array yes May be empty. filters array yes May be empty (an empty ruleset allows everything). comment string no Free-form description.

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
A marker checks one thing about a message and stores the yes/no answer under its id for filters to use.

Field Type Required Notes id string yes Unique across all markers and filters. name string no Label for the UI only. enabled boolean no Defaults to true. scope scope yes Which part of the message to look at (see below). direction direction no Defaults to "both". matcher matcher yes How to test that part (see below).

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
A filter is a rule that can change the verdict. It has every field a marker has, plus:

Field Type Required Notes mode mode yes How a match affects the verdict (see below). needed_markers_all array of ids no The filter runs only if every listed marker matched. needed_markers_any array of ids no The filter runs only if at least one listed marker matched.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text: Mode When the matcher matches When it does not blacklist drop the message immediately keep evaluating the other rules whitelist_all counts as one required hit the message is dropped, a required hit is missing whitelist_any satisfies its group dropped only if no whitelist-any filter in the group matched

docs.title: Directions
docs.text: inbound is client to service, outbound is service to client, and both is either. A rule only runs on messages whose direction matches.

docs.title: Scopes and the matchers they allow
docs.text:
A scope is the part of a message a rule looks at. Each scope only allows certain matchers and, in one case, certain directions. Validation and compilation use this same table, so a ruleset that validates will always compile.

Scope Allowed matchers Allowed directions stream stream_regex, stream_bytes, bytes_hex, size, always any http.path path_regex, size, always any http.body body_regex, body_bytes, bytes_hex, size, always any http.header header_regex, size, always any http.method method_regex, always any http.status status_regex, always outbound or both (never inbound) timing session.lifetime, session.idle, always both only

Any other combination fails validation. In particular: size is not allowed on http.status, http.method, or timing; the byte matchers exist only where raw bytes do (stream and http.body); and timing matchers must run in both directions.

docs.title: Matchers
docs.text:
A matcher object has a "type" field that selects the variant; the other keys are its payload.

type Payload What it does stream_regex pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over the raw stream as text. path_regex pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over the request path. body_regex pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over the body as text. header_regex header_name, pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over a header value; the name is matched case-insensitively. method_regex pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over the HTTP method. status_regex pattern, case_sensitive? Regex over the status code as text; responses only. stream_bytes pattern Binary-safe byte regex over the raw stream (. is any byte, \xNN a literal byte). body_bytes pattern Binary-safe byte regex over the body. bytes_hex value A literal hex signature found anywhere in the scope's bytes, for example "deadbeef" (whitespace allowed). Only on stream or http.body. size op, value, field_name? Compares the size of the scope. field_name only applies to http.header. session.lifetime op, value (seconds) How long the connection has been open. timing scope, both directions. session.idle op, value (seconds) How long since the last message. Same constraints. always value (bool) true always matches, false never. Works with any scope.

op is one of <, <=, ==, !=, >=, >. case_sensitive defaults to false. Regexes use the Rust regex grammar, which is linear-time and has no look-around or back-references; inline (?i) works. Use the byte matchers for binary traffic, where . and \xNN are byte-oriented.

A few matchers on their own:

{ "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/admin", "case_sensitive": false }

{ "type": "size", "op": "<=", "value": 256 }

{ "type": "bytes_hex", "value": "deadbeef" }

{ "type": "session.idle", "op": ">", "value": 2.45 }

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A ruleset is checked before it can take effect, and all problems are reported together rather than one at a time. The checks are:

  1. The shapes must match the tables above; an unknown key is an error.
  2. Every id must be unique across markers and filters.
  3. The combination of scope, matcher, and direction must be allowed by the table above.
  4. Every id in needed_markers_all or needed_markers_any must exist and must name a marker.
  5. A rule may not use a scope the port has disabled (a port can turn specific scopes off).

You can check a ruleset without deploying it through the .../ruleset/validate endpoint (see the API reference).

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text: This page gives you a mental model of sinkhole before the details. Terms in bold have a precise meaning that the rest of the docs rely on, and the Glossary collects them in one place.

docs.title: The filter and the controller
docs.text:
sinkhole is split into two programs with very different jobs.

Filter Controller How many one in front of each guarded service one, central Sees live client and service traffic no traffic, only the filters it manages Does proxy traffic, evaluate rules, record decisions manage filters, collect their data, serve the API Stores its own records and rules a copy of every filter's data

A filter is configured once at startup through environment variables: its ports, the service it forwards to, its token, and a few limits. Everything after that, the rules and any live changes, goes through the controller. You and the web UI only ever talk to the controller, which relays changes to the right filter, and never to a filter directly.

To put a filter under the controller's management, you give the controller the filter's address (its host and port), its token, and a name to refer to it by. From then on you work with that name.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
A message is one complete unit of traffic that the filter evaluates. If the traffic is HTTP and the filter can read a whole request or response, that request or response is the message. Otherwise, for a binary protocol, or a body too large to hold, or one streamed in pieces, the filter works with a raw chunk of bytes instead.

Every message gets a single decision, either Allow or Drop, and produces one evaluation record describing what happened. A Drop does not just discard that one message: the filter tears down the whole connection. That holds in either direction, an inbound request that matches an attack pattern, or an outbound response where the service is leaking something it should not.

A message also has a direction: inbound is client to service, outbound is service to client. A rule can apply to one direction or both.

docs.title: How rules decide
docs.text:
A ruleset belongs to a single port and contains two kinds of rules.

  • Markers look at a message and note whether something is true about it, for example "this request is authenticated" or "this looks like a file upload". A marker never blocks anything on its own. It only records its answer so other rules can use it.
  • Filters are the rules that actually allow or block. A filter can be set to apply only when certain markers were true, so you can say things like "only check this on uploads". Each filter is one of three modes:
    • blacklist: if it matches, the message is dropped.
    • whitelist_all: every whitelist-all filter that applies must match, otherwise the message is dropped.
    • whitelist_any: at least one whitelist-any filter that applies must match, otherwise the message is dropped.

Each rule reads one part of a message, its scope (the path, body, headers, method, status, the raw stream, or timing), and tests it with a matcher (a regex, a byte or hex signature, a size check, a timing check, or a plain "always"). If the part a rule needs is not present in the message, the rule is skipped. A missing field never counts as a match.

The full behavior is in Rule model and Evaluation semantics.

docs.title: Records and events
docs.text:
Two separate streams flow from each filter up to the controller.

  • Evaluation records: one per message. They hold the decision, which markers and filters matched, the reason a message was dropped, the HTTP metadata, and the captured bytes.
  • ECAM events: sinkhole's own operational log, things like configuration errors, network failures, and security warnings. These are separate from per-message records and from ordinary log lines. See ECAM events.

Both are stored on the filter first and pulled into the controller's central database on a schedule. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every request between the web UI, the controller, and the filters carries a bearer token. The controller checks the token on requests it receives, and when it calls a filter it sends that filter's token, so it keeps each filter's token in order to do so. Tokens travel over the control network on every request, which is why that network is meant to be private rather than exposed.

Note

What happens when a token is missing or wrong, and how CORS is handled, is covered in Authentication.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text: This page explains the main design decisions behind sinkhole and why they were made. It is background rather than a how-to. If you just want to run it, start with Core concepts and the Quickstart.

docs.title: Two programs, not one
docs.text:
sinkhole is split into a filter and a controller because they have very different jobs and very different failure modes. A filter sits next to the service it guards, often on a host that can reboot or get compromised, and it has to keep enforcing rules no matter what else is going on. The controller is where a person works: it manages the whole fleet, collects what every filter records, and serves the UI.

Keeping the two apart means the part on the traffic path stays small and focused, while the part with all the moving pieces (a database, a fleet to track, an API) runs separately, off the path of the messages that have to keep flowing. A filter never needs the controller to be reachable in order to keep doing its job.

docs.title: A proxy in front, not a library inside
docs.text:
A filter sits in front of a service and treats it as a black box. It works at the network level, on the service's ports, and does not look inside the service or depend on how it is built. You do not modify, rebuild, or even restart the service to guard it: you reroute its port through the filter. That makes sinkhole behave the same way regardless of what the service is written in, and it means a filter can be added or removed without touching the thing it protects.

The one thing a filter may need from the service is its TLS certificate and key, so it can terminate TLS and see the traffic in the clear. That is still a network concern, not knowledge of the service's logic.

docs.title: Open by default, tightened live
docs.text:
A fresh filter has no rules and forwards everything unchanged. This is deliberate. Installing the filter should never be the thing that takes a service down, and you should not have to write rules before the service can come up. You bring the filter up first, confirm traffic still flows, then add rules while it runs.

Note

The trade-off is that a filter with no rules protects nothing. Open by default is about deployment order, not security. The protection comes from the rules you add afterwards.

docs.title: Rust on the path
docs.text: Every message, in both directions, is parsed and run through the ruleset before it is allowed onward. That work sits directly between the client and the service, so it has to be fast and its latency has to be steady. The filter is written in Rust for that reason, and the engine keeps the per-message cost low: regular expressions run in linear time, with no catastrophic backtracking on hostile input, and a filter is evaluated only when its markers say it applies, so most messages touch only a few rules.

docs.title: Changing rules without downtime
docs.text: In a live game you rewrite rules constantly. If applying a new ruleset dropped connections or briefly stopped traffic, you would think twice before touching the rules at all, which is the opposite of what a tool for reacting quickly should do. So a port's rules are swapped while traffic keeps flowing, and the change does not tear down existing connections.

docs.title: The controller pulls, it does not hold the filters up
docs.text:
The controller polls each filter for its records, events, and health. Filters do not depend on the controller to keep enforcing, and the controller does not depend on a filter reaching out to it. If the controller goes down, the filters carry on with the rules they already have. When a filter restarts, it restores its last ruleset from its local database on boot, so it comes back up already enforcing the same rules rather than empty.

Because of this, a controller outage does not loosen any filter. The filters keep enforcing whether or not the controller is reachable. The controller is there to manage and observe the fleet, not to keep it running.

docs.title: Recognize, then decide
docs.text: Rules come in two kinds on purpose. Markers recognize a situation, such as "this request is authenticated" or "this looks like an upload", without deciding anything. Filters make the allow-or-block call, and can be limited to apply only when certain markers held. Splitting recognition from decision lets you describe a condition once and reuse it, instead of repeating the same detection inside every rule.

docs.title: Decide once, record everything
docs.text: Every message produces a record: the decision, the rule that caused it, and the bytes involved. Knowing that something was blocked is not enough during attack and defense. You need to see what it was and why. Visibility is treated as a feature rather than a debugging aid, which is why records are structured and stream to the controller as traffic happens.

docs.title: A small, private control plane
docs.text: The control API a filter exposes is reached only by the controller, over a network meant to be private. It is not built for browsers, and the web UI never talks to it. Operators authenticate to the controller, the controller authenticates to each filter, and the trust boundary stays in one place.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
In production each filter runs on the host it guards, and a single controller runs on an admin host and reaches the filters over a trusted control network. The test compose file is not a production topology.

Installing in front of a service

The usual way to put a filter in front of a service is to reroute its published port through the filter, a small edit to the service's Compose file, or the autoconfigurer that does it for you. See Installing a filter. This page covers the wider production setup.

flowchart LR
    subgraph admin["Admin host"]
      CTRL["controller :7000"]
    end
    subgraph hostA["Guarded host A"]
      FA["filter :7001 (control)"]
      SA["service"]
      FA --> SA
    end
    subgraph hostB["Guarded host B"]
      FB["filter :7001 (control)"]
      SB["service"]
      FB --> SB
    end
    CTRL -->|control API, bearer| FA
    CTRL -->|control API, bearer| FB
    netA(["clients"]) --> FA
    netB(["clients"]) --> FB

docs.title: Getting the binaries
docs.text:
The repository's Dockerfile builds both binaries and produces a runtime image for each:

docker build --target filter     -t sinkhole-filter .
docker build --target controller -t sinkhole-controller .

You can also run the plain binaries; they are configured the same way, through environment variables. Either way the filter's control API defaults to port 7001 and the controller's API to 7000, both with DEBUG=false.

Two ways to ship the web UI

The release binaries (built by scripts/build_release.sh) embed the web UI directly into the controller, so a single binary serves both the API and the UI (SERVE_FRONTEND is on by default; see Web UI). The Docker image above does not bundle the UI (it keeps the image lean and the build fast); run it with a separate frontend and SERVE_FRONTEND=false, as the controller example below does.

docs.title: Deploy a filter
docs.text:
On each guarded host:

docker run -d --name sinkhole-filter \
  -e SINKHOLE_FILTER_UPSTREAM_HOST=127.0.0.1 \
  -e SINKHOLE_FILTER_LISTEN_MAP="80:8080" \
  -e SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONTROL_BIND="0.0.0.0:7001" \
  -e SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN_HASH="$(printf '%s' "$FILTER_TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
  -v sinkhole-data:/app/sinkhole-data \
  -p 80:80 -p 7001:7001 \
  sinkhole-filter

Things to get right:

  • Expose the data ports to clients, but keep the control port reachable only by the controller (a private network or a firewall rule). It is not a public endpoint.
  • The filter only ever sees the token hash. Keep the plaintext for the controller's service config.
  • To guard an HTTPS service, give the filter the service's certificate and key with TLS_MAP. See TLS termination.
  • Put the filter's database on a volume (mount sinkhole-data/ or set DB_PATH), and keep hydration on (the default) so the filter re-enforces its last ruleset after a reboot. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: Deploy the controller
docs.text:
On the admin host:

docker run -d --name sinkhole-controller \
  -e SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_BIND="0.0.0.0:7000" \
  -e SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_AUTH_TOKEN="$CTRL_TOKEN" \
  -e SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVE_FRONTEND="false" \
  -e SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_CORS_ORIGIN="https://admin.example.com" \
  -e SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES='[{"id":"edge","url":"http://10.0.0.5:7001","token":"'"$FILTER_TOKEN"'"}]' \
  -v sinkhole-data:/app/sinkhole-data \
  -p 7000:7000 \
  sinkhole-controller

The Docker image has no embedded UI, so this disables the bundled UI and points CORS at the separate frontend you serve. If you instead run a release binary, drop both of those lines: the UI is bundled and served same-origin by default (see Web UI).

Things to get right:

  • In production the controller refuses to start without an auth token. It also requires a CORS origin unless it is serving the bundled UI. Here the UI is decoupled, so set the frontend's origin explicitly. See Authentication.
  • Each service's token is that filter's plaintext token; its sha256 must equal the filter's AUTH_TOKEN_HASH.
  • You do not have to declare every filter here. Services can be added, removed, and reconfigured through the API at runtime, and the controller remembers where it left off, so a re-added service resumes instead of re-pulling its history.
  • Tune RETENTION_FILTER_SECS, RETENTION_DB_SECS, and PRUNE_INTERVAL_SECS for your disk budget. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
The controller can serve the operator web UI itself, or you can run it separately. The two modes are mutually exclusive in practice and differ only in SERVE_FRONTEND and CORS_ORIGIN.

Bundled (default). A release binary embeds the UI and serves it under /ui on the controller's own port, same origin as the API. Just open http://<controller-host>:7000, which redirects to /ui/. Because it is same-origin, no CORS is involved (cross-origin requests are denied), so you do not set CORS_ORIGIN. This is the simplest deployment: one binary, one port, one token.

Decoupled. Set SERVE_FRONTEND=false and host the frontend elsewhere (the Docker image, a static host, or the Vite dev server). The browser then calls the controller cross-origin, so you must set CORS_ORIGIN to the frontend's origin. Build the static assets with cd frontend && npm run build and serve frontend/dist however you like.

Either way the API itself is unchanged and still requires the controller's bearer token; serving the UI does not expose anything new.

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
• Never run with DEBUG=true in production. It disables the no-token guard and makes CORS permissive.
  • Keep filter control APIs off the public internet.
  • Give the controller's own API a strong token. If you run a decoupled frontend, also set a strict CORS_ORIGIN; the bundled UI is same-origin and needs none.

The full variable list is in Environment variables.

docs.title: Installing a filter
docs.text: Putting sinkhole in front of a service is a change to its Docker Compose file: you route the service's published port through a filter container that forwards to the original service. There is no code change and no rebuild, just an edit to the compose file, and it is easy to automate.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A service usually publishes its port straight to the host:

flowchart LR
    C(["clients"]) -->|"host :1337"| CH["service :1337"]

sinkhole inserts itself in between. The filter takes over the published host port and forwards to the service over the internal Compose network. The service stops publishing to the host and becomes reachable only from inside:

flowchart LR
    C(["clients"]) -->|"host :1337"| F["filter :1337"]
    F -->|"service:1337 (internal net)"| CH["service :1337"]
    CTRL["controller"] -->|"control :7001"| F

From the outside nothing changes: same host, same port. The filter relays bytes exactly, so a filter with no rules behaves the same as the bare service.

docs.title: The Compose edit
docs.text:
There are two changes. Stop the service from publishing to the host, exposing it on the internal network only, and add a filter service that publishes the port and forwards to the service.

Before, the service's own compose:

services:
  service:
    image: my-service
    ports:
      - "1337:1337"     # host -> service, directly

After:

services:
  service:
    image: my-service
    expose:
      - "1337"          # internal network only; no longer host-published

  sinkhole-filter:
    image: sinkhole-filter
    depends_on: [service]
    environment:
      SINKHOLE_FILTER_UPSTREAM_HOST: service           # the Compose service name
      SINKHOLE_FILTER_LISTEN_MAP: "1337:1337"          # public:upstream
      SINKHOLE_FILTER_CONTROL_BIND: "0.0.0.0:7001"
      SINKHOLE_FILTER_AUTH_TOKEN_HASH: "${FILTER_HASH}"
    volumes:
      - ./sinkhole-data:/sinkhole-data
    ports:
      - "1337:1337"     # host -> filter (was the service's)
      - "7001:7001"     # control API, reachable by the controller only

That is the whole installation. docker compose up now brings the service up behind the filter. The test stack is a working example of this shape.

docs.title: Doing it automatically
docs.text:
You do not have to make this edit by hand. sinkhole ships an autoconfigurer that reads a service's Compose file, finds its published ports, rewrites them to run through a filter, and writes the result back, keeping a .bak of the original. It shows the before-and-after port plan and asks for confirmation before writing. A companion tool produces a self-signed certificate for a TLS port from an existing private key. Both are small command-line tools shipped with a release, meant to be copied onto the box you are deploying on.

Note

For a box that exposes several ports across different services, the autoconfigurer routes each port to its own upstream, so a single filter can guard the whole box.

docs.title: Open by default
docs.text:
The filter is configured entirely through environment variables (see Environment variables), so the moment the stack comes up the filter is already running and forwarding. It just has no rules yet, so it passes everything. An empty ruleset means open.

The order is simple: bring the stack up, and the service is immediately reachable through the filter (open); then add rules through the controller whenever you want, and the filter starts enforcing them. Installing the filter and writing the rules are separate steps, so installing it never takes the service down and never blocks traffic before you have written anything. Rules are added and changed under live traffic, with no downtime (see live reload).

docs.title: Wiring it to the controller
docs.text:
The filter now serves traffic on its own. To manage it from the controller, make its control port (7001) reachable from the admin host, and register the filter as a service, either in the controller's configuration or at runtime through the API, using the filter's address and token. The name you give it there is how you refer to this filter from then on. See Deployment and Authentication.

Warning

Publish the data port or ports to clients, but keep the control port off the public internet. Restrict it to the controller's network. It is a management endpoint, not part of the service.

docs.title: Testing and development
docs.text: Dev tasks live in the justfile (run just to list them). Cargo commands are workspace-wide.

docs.title: Build, test, lint
docs.text:
just build                    # cargo build --workspace
just test                     # cargo test --workspace
cargo test -p filter <name>   # run a single test (crate + name filter)
just check                    # cargo check --workspace
just fmt                      # cargo fmt --all
just clippy                   # cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets

CI (.github/workflows/build_test.yaml) runs two jobs:

  • lint: cargo fmt --all --check and cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings. A warning fails the build.
  • build and test: cargo build and cargo test on stable, beta, and nightly.

docs.title: The test stack
docs.text:
The test stack brings up a few mock services, a filter in front of each, and one controller, all on a single Docker network. It is self-contained, with tokens baked in.

docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yaml up --build   # or: just up
docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yaml down -v       # or: just down

See the Quickstart for what it contains and how to drive it through the controller.

docs.title: Driving traffic
docs.text:
Two small Python clients (standard library only) under docker/traffic/ exercise a running stack from the outside, the way a real client or checker would.

  • just traffic [ARGS] runs traffic_client.py: send individual requests to poke rules live and watch each allow or drop decision.
  • just stress [ARGS] runs stress_client.py: fire parallel load at one or many services at once, to see how the proxy and the database hold up under pressure.

Both talk to the public data ports, so they show what an attacker or the game's checker would see. To inspect what the filter decided, read the records back through the controller.

docs.title: OpenAPI specs
docs.text:
The committed specs in docs/assets/openapi/ (and the Swagger reference pages), plus the frontend's generated types, are derived from the code. After changing any API request or response type, or any route:

just regen-openapi   # boots both binaries and writes fresh OpenAPI JSON into docs/

Keep the regenerated JSON with the code change so the API reference and the UI types stay in sync.

docs.title: Manual API exploration
docs.text: Both binaries serve Swagger UI at /docs and the raw spec at /openapi.json, so you can exercise endpoints interactively (a bearer token is required for protected routes). A Postman or Hurl collection works equally well against the controller API.

docs.title: Where tests live
docs.text:
• Rule engine decisions: filter/src/engine/dispatcher.rs.
  • HTTP parser edge cases: filter/src/http/parser.rs.
  • Matchers and rule legality: filter/src/matcher/ and filter/src/rules/.
  • Token hashing and base types: shared/src/.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
sinkhole exposes two HTTP APIs, shown here from the committed OpenAPI specs (generated from the code):

  • Controller API: the operator and UI-facing API. This is the one you normally use; it relays edits to filters and serves the aggregated data.
  • Filter API: the per-filter control API the controller calls. Useful for understanding the data flow or debugging a single filter.

Each running process also serves Swagger UI at /docs and the raw spec at /openapi.json.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Auth: protected endpoints need Authorization: Bearer <token>, the controller token for the controller API and the filter token for the filter API. See Authentication.
  • Success responses are wrapped as {"status":"ok","data":{...}}.
  • Errors are wrapped as {"status":"error","code":<http>,"title":"...","detail":"..."}.
  • List endpoints for records and events return a next_since cursor to page forward. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: ECAM events
docs.text:
ECAM is sinkhole's structured operational event log: the things worth an operator's attention, such as configuration errors, network failures, security warnings, and database problems. It is separate from two other streams:

  • evaluation records, the per-message allow and drop decisions (see Evaluation semantics);
  • ordinary log lines, the free-form developer output on stdout.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: A filter writes events into a small in-memory buffer (capped, with the oldest dropped when it fills). The controller pulls each filter's events on the SYNC_ECAM_INTERVAL_MS cadence, using a per-filter cursor, and stores them centrally so the UI can show one event feed for the whole fleet. See Data and persistence.

docs.title: Event shape
docs.text:
{
  "ts_ns":    1754004005155452000,
  "severity": "warn",
  "origin":   { "Network": { "ClientToFilter": 8080 } },
  "msg":      "TLS handshake failed on port 8080",
  "data":     null
}
Field Type Meaning ts_ns u64 Event time, in nanoseconds. severity "warn" or "error" How serious it is. origin enum Which part of the system raised it (see below). msg string Human-readable description. data JSON or absent Optional structured payload; omitted when there is none.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
There are two levels, because ECAM is for the noteworthy, not for routine debugging:

  • warn: degraded but recoverable, such as an upstream that was briefly unreachable or a dropped TLS handshake.
  • error: a real fault, such as a misconfiguration, a port that failed to bind, a database write failure, or a security problem.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text:
origin says which part of the system raised the event.

Origin Raised by Global process-wide events Configuration environment and config validation problems Network accept, connect, and TLS issues (carries a per-port detail) Port a specific public port Matcher a specific rule on a port (carries the port and rule id) DB local database problems API control-API handling Telemetry the record pipeline Security authentication and authorization events

docs.title: Reading events
docs.text:
• From one filter directly: GET /ecam, paging with the since cursor.
  • Aggregated through the controller: GET /ecam, or GET /services/{service}/ecam for a single filter.

Events are ordered oldest first, and each response carries a next_since cursor to page forward. See the API reference.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition Why it exists Filter The proxy that guards one service: it forwards traffic and runs the rules on it. The thing that actually allows or drops bytes. See Filter. Controller The single orchestrator that manages a fleet of filters. One place to push rules and collect data. See Controller. Service One managed filter as the controller knows it (id, url, token). The controller's unit of management. Service id The stable name you use to refer to a managed filter in the controller; it appears in API paths and database keys. How you address a filter. See Identifiers. Service name An optional display label for a service. Shown in the UI; never addresses anything. Message One unit of evaluated traffic: a full HTTP request or response, or a raw chunk when the traffic is not HTTP. The thing a decision is made for. Direction inbound (client to service), outbound (service to client), or both. Lets a rule target one flow (a status check, for instance, only makes sense outbound). Scope Which part of a message a rule reads: stream, http.path, http.body, http.header, http.method, http.status, or timing. Keeps matchers simple and reusable. Matcher The test a rule runs: regex, byte or hex signature, size, session timing, or always. The actual test logic, under a stable JSON shape. Marker A rule that only records whether something is true; it never decides. Check a fact once and gate many filters on it. Filter rule A rule that can allow or block; it runs after markers and can be limited to apply only when given markers held. Carries the actual block or allow logic. Gating Limiting a filter to apply only when certain markers held (needed_markers_all, needed_markers_any). Express logic like "A and (B or C)". Mode How a filter's match affects the verdict: blacklist, whitelist_all, whitelist_any. Describes what a hit means. Decision The verdict for a message: allow or drop. Forward, or tear down and record. Drop reason The structured reason attached to a drop (blacklist, whitelist-all miss, whitelist-any miss). Lets the UI show why something was blocked. Evaluation record The full per-message record: decision, markers, drop reason, per-rule detail, HTTP metadata, and captured bytes. The analyzable output, stored and centralized. ECAM sinkhole's operational event log (severity, origin, message). Operator-facing health and security events, separate from records. See ECAM. Ruleset The per-port JSON document of markers and filters. The unit that is deployed and reloaded. See Rule model. Hydration Restoring a filter's ruleset and config from its local database on boot. A filter re-enforces its rules after a restart, on its own. Cursor How far the controller has pulled records or events from a filter. Resume after a restart instead of re-pulling history. Pruner The controller loop that trims already-copied records on filters and applies retention to the central database. Keeps storage bounded on both ends. See persistence. Sink A consumer of a filter's output (records to the database and stdout; events to the ECAM buffer). Separates producing records and events from storing them.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
When you work with sinkhole you deal with three kinds of identifier. They are easy to mix up, so here is what each one is and where you use it.

Identifier What it is Where you use it Address (host and port) where something listens on the network clients connect to a filter's data port; the controller reaches a filter at its control address Service id the name you give the controller for a managed filter every controller API path, and the UI Display name a human-friendly label for a service the UI only

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
These are ordinary network addresses.

  • Clients connect to a filter's public data ports (the public side of LISTEN_MAP), and the filter forwards to the service behind it.
  • The controller reaches each filter at its control address (the filter's CONTROL_BIND, default port 7001), and the web UI reaches the controller at its BIND (default port 7000).

docs.title: Service id
docs.text:
When you register a filter with the controller you give it an id. That id is how you refer to the filter from then on: it appears in every controller API path (for example PUT /services/edge/ports/8080/ruleset), it keys the filter's records and cursors in the central database, and it is how the UI lists and selects filters.

You set it in the controller's SINKHOLE_CONTROLLER_SERVICES, along with the filter's control url and token:

[{"id":"edge","url":"http://10.0.0.5:7001","token":"…","name":"Edge filter"}]

The id maps to the url and token, which is what actually tells the controller how to reach the filter. Because the id stays stable, a filter can change its address (move hosts) without losing its history.

docs.title: Display name
docs.text: The optional name is just a label shown in the UI. You can set it when you register the filter and change it later through the API, along with a description, color, and icon. It never addresses anything, and it can change freely.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
For a filter guarding a service on 10.0.0.5, published on port 1337 and registered as edge:

  • clients connect to 10.0.0.5:1337, the data address;
  • the controller talks to http://10.0.0.5:7001, the control address;
  • you operate it as /services/edge/..., the service id.

It is the same filter; you just refer to it differently depending on whether you are a client, the controller, or an operator.

See the API reference and Environment variables.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This brings the whole system up on one machine and walks through the operator path: deploy a ruleset through the controller, send a request, and watch it get dropped.

The local stack is docker-compose.test.yaml. It is self-contained: every token is baked into the file, so there is nothing to set up first.

Test topology only

This stack runs everything on a single Docker network for convenience. In a real deployment the filters and the controller run on separate machines. See Deployment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker, with the Compose plugin (docker compose).
  • Optional: just and a Rust toolchain. just wraps the same Docker commands and is shown next to them below.

docs.title: 1. Bring up the stack
docs.text:
Dockerjust 
docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yaml up --build

just up

This starts a handful of mock services, one filter in front of each, and the controller (its API is on port 7000). One of those services is gadget: an echo server you can reach through its filter on port 6001.

When you are done, tear it down:

Dockerjust 
docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yaml down -v

just down

docs.title: 2. Deploy a ruleset
docs.text:
Everything goes through the controller. This blocks any request whose path starts with /blocked, on the gadget service, port 6001.

Note

This is the raw API call. In normal use the web UI builds and sends it for you, so you would not type this by hand. It is shown so you can see what the UI does under the hood, and so you can script the controller if you want to.

CTRL=http://localhost:7000
TOKEN=token-controller-897fe79a   # baked into docker-compose.test.yaml

curl -fsS -X PUT "$CTRL/services/gadget/ports/6001/ruleset" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
        "comment": "demo",
        "markers": [],
        "filters": [
          { "id": "no-blocked", "mode": "blacklist", "direction": "inbound",
            "scope": "http.path",
            "matcher": { "type": "path_regex", "pattern": "^/blocked" } }
        ]
      }'

docs.title: 3. Send traffic through the filter
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:6001/          # allowed: the echo service replies 200
curl -i http://localhost:6001/blocked   # dropped: the connection closes with no reply

docs.title: 4. See the decision in the controller
docs.text:
The controller pulls records from each filter on a short interval. After a moment:

curl -fsS "$CTRL/services/gadget/ports/6001/records?decision=drop&limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

You get the drop record for /blocked, including the filter that matched and the structured reason it was dropped.
